label: echoed first token y at the first copy step (t = L+1)
explanation: Fires almost only at step t = L+1, the first copy step after <DEL>, when the input is the fed-back first original token and that token is y, so first_tok = y. It outputs original token 1. Magnitude grows with sequence length: it does not fire for L = 3-4, is weak for L = 5 (1.6% of mass, many L=5 cases inactive) and strongest for L = 8-9. It does not fire in the original phase (apart from a tiny tail of y as the last original token), at the delimiter step, on y at later copy steps (only trace activations at recall_idx 2 when y is original token 1), or on any other token at the first copy step. Output token and later context have no effect.

issues: The test scores reproduce exactly: P=0.918, R=0.984, F1=0.950, mass recall 0.999.

The false positives are all at L=5, which is the borderline case the explanation describes. (recall_idx==1)&(in_tok==y)&(L==5) has precision 0.58 and holds 1.5% of activation mass. Splitting it by in_count, digits vs letters in the output token, correct, n_digits and out_tok found no clean condition that separates firing from non-firing. Even out_tok==y reached only 0.86 precision and covers almost no events, so this looks like a magnitude threshold, not a missing variable.
With L>=6 the predicate has precision 1.0, recall 0.862 and mass recall 0.984 (F1 0.926). This matches the claim and confirms that L=5 is the only source of false positives.
Magnitude growing with L checks out. Active counts are similar at about 2.8k each for L=6-9, while mass share rises 0.14, 0.24, 0.29, 0.32. L=3-4 has zero activations.

The missed activations (207 on test, 0.1% of mass) are all tiny (up to 0.12 of max) at recall_idx 2 where y is original token 1, as the explanation says. On dev there are 45 tiny original-phase activations at orig_idx 7-8, near the end of the original phase, and none at the delimiter step.
Minor wording point: the label says 'first copy step (t = L+1)'. With this indexing that is the step where recall_idx==1, so the input is the fed-back orig(0). That is consistent, not an error.
